- MUST use landmarks: one `<main>`, plus `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<footer>`, `<aside>` where they apply. Label multiple navs (`aria-label="Primary"`).
- MUST have one `<h1>` per page and headings in order without skipped levels. Heading level follows structure, not font size; style any level to look as needed.
- Buttons do things (`<button>`); links go places (`<a href>`). NEVER put a click handler on a `<div>` or `<span>`. An `<a>` without `href` is not focusable.
- Lists of things are `<ul>`/`<ol>`; tabular data is a `<table>` with `<th scope>` and a caption or accessible name (1.3.1).
- Set `lang` on `<html>` (3.1.1) and on passages in another language (3.1.2).
- DOM order MUST match visual reading order (1.3.2, 2.4.3). Don't rearrange with CSS `order`, grid placement or absolute positioning in a way that changes meaning.

### Keyboard

- Everything operable by pointer MUST be operable by keyboard (2.1.1), with no keyboard traps (2.1.2).
- Tab order follows reading order. Don't use positive `tabindex`; use `tabindex="0"` only to make custom widgets focusable and `-1` for elements you focus by script.
- Focus MUST be visible (2.4.7) and not hidden behind sticky headers or footers (2.4.11). Style with `:focus-visible`; the indicator needs 3:1 contrast against its surroundings and should be at least a 2px outline. Never remove outlines without a replacement.
- Content-heavy pages and pages with long nav SHOULD have a skip link to `<main>` as the first focusable element, visible on focus (2.4.1).
- Composite widgets (tabs, menus, listboxes, grids) use one tab stop and arrow keys inside, following established keyboard patterns for that widget.
- Dragging MUST have a single-pointer alternative, such as move buttons or a menu (2.5.7).

### Focus management

- Dialogs: use `<dialog>` with `showModal()` where possible (it makes the page inert and closes on Escape). On open, move focus to the first meaningful control or the dialog heading; keep focus inside while open; on close, return focus to the element that opened it.
- Menus and popovers: Escape closes and returns focus to the trigger. The trigger has `aria-expanded`.
- After deleting an item or changing route in a single-page app, move focus somewhere sensible (the next item, the new page's `<h1>`), never to `<body>`.

### Accessible names

- Every control MUST have an accessible name (4.1.2). Prefer visible text: a `<label for>` for fields, button text for buttons.
- Use `aria-label` only when there is no visible text, such as icon-only buttons (`aria-label="Close"`). Icon-only buttons SHOULD also have a tooltip for sighted users.
- When there is visible text, the accessible name MUST contain it, ideally starting with it (2.5.3), so voice users can say what they see.
- Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; inline SVGs that convey meaning get a title or name.

### ARIA

- No ARIA is better than bad ARIA. A native element already has the right role, states and keyboard behaviour; use it before adding roles.
- ARIA changes what is announced, not behaviour. If you add `role="button"`, you also owe focusability, Enter and Space handling, and a name.
- Never put `aria-hidden="true"` on anything focusable. Keep states in sync (`aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-pressed`, `aria-current`).

### Images and alt text

- Informative images: alt text that says what the image communicates in context, not "image of". Decorative images: `alt=""`.
- Images of text are avoided; when unavoidable, the alt contains the text. Charts need a text summary or a data table.

### Forms

- Every field has a visible, programmatically associated label (3.3.2). Placeholder is not a label.
- Group related controls (radio sets, address blocks) with `<fieldset>` and `<legend>`.
- Errors: identify the field and describe the problem in text (3.3.1) with a suggestion where possible (3.3.3). Link the message with `aria-describedby`, set `aria-invalid="true"` on the field, and on submit move focus to an error summary that links to each field (or to the first invalid field on a short form).
- Use correct `type` and `autocomplete` values so browsers and password managers can fill fields; don't ask for the same information twice in one process (3.3.7). Never block paste into password or code fields (3.3.8).

### Live regions

- Status messages that appear without focus moving (saved, results count, upload progress) MUST be announced (4.1.3): put them in a region with `role="status"` or `aria-live="polite"` that exists in the DOM before the message is inserted.
- Use `role="alert"` (assertive) only for urgent errors. Don't announce every keystroke; debounce.

### Color and contrast

- Text MUST meet the floor: 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text (1.4.3). Check text over images and gradients at the worst point.
- Non-text elements people need to see (field borders, icons that carry meaning, chart marks, focus indicators, control states) MUST have 3:1 against adjacent colors (1.4.11).
- Color MUST NOT be the only signal (1.4.1): errors get an icon and text; links in body text get an underline or another non-color cue.

### Motion and flashing

- Honour `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: replace movement, parallax and auto-playing animation with fades or no animation (see `motion.md`).
- NEVER flash anything more than three times in any one-second period (2.3.1).
- Auto-moving content that lasts more than five seconds (carousels, tickers) MUST have pause (2.2.2).

### Zoom and reflow

- Text MUST resize to 200% without loss (1.4.4); content MUST reflow at 320 CSS px wide (equivalent to 400% zoom at 1280px) without two-dimensional scrolling, except for content that needs it, such as data tables and maps (1.4.10). Use `rem` for type and avoid fixed heights on text containers.
- Layout MUST survive user text spacing overrides (1.4.12): no clipped text when line height, letter spacing or word spacing increase.
- Hover and focus content (tooltips, popovers) must be dismissible with Escape, hoverable, and stay until dismissed (1.4.13).

### Target size

- Targets MUST be at least 24×24 CSS px, or have enough spacing that a 24px circle on each doesn't overlap another (2.5.8, AA). Inline links in text are exempt. Use 44×44px on touch surfaces (see `responsive.md`).

### Contrast modes

- Respect `forced-colors: active`: don't convey state only with background or box-shadow (they are removed); use borders or outlines, which take system colors. If a custom focus style uses `box-shadow`, add `outline: 2px solid transparent` too; forced-colors mode removes the shadow but paints the outline in a system color.
- Optionally strengthen borders and muted text under `prefers-contrast: more`.

## Generic defaults to catch

- **`outline: none` with no replacement** → keyboard users lose their place → `:focus-visible` style with 3:1 contrast.
- **Div buttons and icon buttons with no name** → silent or unreachable → `<button>` with text or `aria-label`.
- **Light gray placeholder as the only label** → fails contrast and vanishes → visible label.
- **ARIA roles sprinkled on native elements** → redundant or conflicting → remove them.
- **Modal that doesn't trap or return focus** → users tab into the page behind.

## Check

- [ ] Landmarks present; one `<h1>`; headings in order; `lang` set.
- [ ] Every interactive element reachable and operable by Tab, Enter, Space, Escape and arrows where expected.
- [ ] Focus always visible, never hidden under sticky elements.
- [ ] Dialogs move focus in, contain it, close on Escape and return focus.
- [ ] Every control has a name containing its visible label.
- [ ] Field errors are linked with `aria-describedby` and `aria-invalid`; async status announced politely.
- [ ] Text 4.5:1 (large 3:1); UI parts and focus indicators 3:1; nothing by color alone.
- [ ] Reduced motion honoured; nothing flashes more than three times a second.
- [ ] Page works at 320 CSS px and 200% text; targets ≥24×24px.
- [ ] Visual order matches DOM order.

references/apps-and-data.md

# Apps and data

Operate mode in depth: app shells, tables, filters, forms, dashboards and settings. Here people come back daily to get work done, so speed, predictability and density beat expression. Personality lives in type, color and one signature detail (see `principles.md`), never in reinvented controls.

## Decide

1. **What are the three most frequent tasks on this screen?** They get the primary positions; everything else goes one level down.
2. **How often, and how expert, are the users?** Daily experts want density and shortcuts; occasional users want labels, space and guidance.
3. **What decision does this data support?** A dashboard or table exists to answer a question. Write the question before choosing a component.
4. **What already exists?** Inherit the shell, table and form patterns of the codebase (see `extend.md`). Never introduce a second table style.

## Rules

### App shell

- SHOULD follow convention: primary navigation in a left sidebar (many sections, or sections that grow) or a top bar (five or fewer stable sections). Account and settings sit at a far end of the nav.
- Every page SHOULD have a header with the page title, an optional one-line context, and the primary action at the end of the header row. One primary action per page; others are secondary or in an overflow menu.
- The current location MUST be indicated by more than color (weight, a marker, `aria-current="page"`).
- Keep the shell stable: nav, header height and action positions don't move between pages.

### Density

- Choose density from task and frequency, not taste: monitoring and bulk editing → compact; occasional review → comfortable. Offer a density toggle only when both audiences really exist.
- Density changes row height and padding, never text below the readable minimum or targets below 24×24px.

### Tables

- Text columns align left; numbers align right with tabular numerals (`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`) so digits line up; headers align with their column's content.
- Keep units and precision consistent within a column; put the unit in the header, not in every cell.
- Header row SHOULD be sticky in any table taller than the viewport. The first column (the row's identity) SHOULD be sticky when the table scrolls sideways.
- Row height: around 28–36px compact, 40–48px comfortable (`space-and-layout.md`), taller only when rows hold two lines or avatars. Pick one per table.
- Use either thin dividers or zebra striping, not both. Dividers suit most tables; zebra helps wide tables with many columns where the eye tracks across.
- Truncate long text with an ellipsis only where the full value is available on hover and on keyboard focus (title alone is not keyboard-accessible), or in the row detail. Never truncate numbers, IDs or amounts.
- Sortable headers are buttons with a visible sort indicator on the active column and `aria-sort` on its header cell.
- Selection: a checkbox column with a header checkbox for select-all (with an indeterminate state), and a bulk action bar showing the count ("3 selected") that replaces or sits over the table toolbar.
- Row states: loading uses skeleton rows of the real row height; an empty table shows the empty state inside the table frame (see `copy.md`); a failed load shows the error and a retry in place. Row actions on hover MUST also be reachable by keyboard and on touch.

### Filters and search

- Active filters MUST be visible as removable chips or a summary line, with a "Clear all". A hidden active filter makes the data look wrong.
- Show the result count, and update it as filters change. Show per-option counts when they help people avoid empty results.
- Search SHOULD filter as you type (debounced) for local data; for slow queries, search on Enter and show progress.
- Filter and sort state SHOULD live in the URL so views can be shared and survive reload.

### Forms in apps

- Group related fields under short headings; order them as the user thinks about the task, not as the database stores them.
- Inline edit suits single values edited often (a name, a status). Use a form or panel when several fields must change together or need validation across fields.
- Pick one save model per surface and make it obvious. **Autosave**: show "Saving…" then "Saved", and never also show a Save button. **Explicit save**: a Save button, a visible unsaved-changes indicator, and a warning before leaving with unsaved changes.

### Dashboards

- Start from the decisions users make ("Which accounts need attention today?"), then show the data that answers each one. Don't start from a row of KPI cards.
- A single number needs context to mean anything: comparison to a previous period or a target, and the time range.
- Choose the chart by the question:

| Question | Chart |
|---|---|
| Compare categories | Bar, sorted by value, horizontal if labels are long |
| Trend over time | Line; bars for few discrete periods |
| Part of a whole | Stacked bar or a single 100% bar; pie only for 2–4 slices |
| Distribution | Histogram, box plot, dot/strip plot |
| Relationship | Scatter |

- Label lines and bars directly at their ends instead of a distant legend when there are few series. Start bar axes at zero. Show units and time range.
- Color: categorical palettes for unordered categories (keep to a handful you can tell apart), sequential (one hue, light to dark) for ordered magnitude, diverging (two hues around a meaningful midpoint) for above/below a reference.
- NEVER rely on color alone to separate series or states: add labels, patterns, markers or position. Distinguish series by lightness as well as hue, so they survive color-vision deficiency and grayscale.
- Every chart has a text alternative: a summary sentence or an accessible data table.

### Settings

- Group by what users are trying to change, with a clear heading per group. Long settings use a section nav.
- Each setting: label, one line on what it affects, current value visible. Toggles apply immediately; grouped fields share one save.

### Destructive actions

- Prefer undo over confirmation for reversible actions ("Archived. Undo").
- Confirm only what can't be undone. The dialog names the object and the consequence ("Delete project 'Atlas'? 214 files will be removed permanently."), and the confirm button repeats the verb ("Delete project"). For high-stakes deletes, ask the user to type the name.
- Destructive buttons use the danger color plus a clear label; never the default focus in the dialog.

### Keyboard, command palette, notifications

- Offer shortcuts for frequent actions and show them in menus and tooltips. Don't override browser or assistive-technology shortcuts. Single-key shortcuts MUST be possible to turn off or remap, or work only when the relevant element has focus (WCAG 2.1.4).
- A command palette suits apps with many actions or objects; it searches both, shows shortcuts beside results, and opens with no animation, because keyboard-triggered UI should appear instantly (see `motion.md`).
- Notifications: confirm in place where the change is visible; use a toast only for background results or undo; reserve banners for persistent system state; never interrupt with a modal for information.

## Generic defaults to catch

- **A row of four gradient stat cards with icons and "+12%" badges** → the default dashboard opening, often with invented numbers → start from decisions; show context; NEVER invent figures.
- **Donut charts for everything** → hard to compare → pick the chart from the question table.
- **Centered numbers in tables, no tabular numerals** → digits don't line up → right-align with tabular numerals.
- **Every action as a primary button** → no hierarchy → one primary per page.
- **Rainbow chart palettes** → color without meaning → categorical, sequential or diverging on purpose.
- **Custom-styled dropdowns, toggles and date pickers** → novelty where people expect convention → native or established components.

## Check

- [ ] One primary action per page, in the header row.
- [ ] Numbers right-aligned with tabular numerals; text left-aligned.
- [ ] Long tables have sticky headers; truncated cells reveal the full value on hover and focus.
- [ ] Active filters visible with counts and "Clear all"; state in the URL.
- [ ] Empty, loading and error states exist for every table and chart.
- [ ] Each dashboard element answers a written question; each number has context.
- [ ] No chart relies on color alone; few series are labelled directly.
- [ ] Irreversible actions confirm with the object named; reversible ones offer undo.
- [ ] One save model per surface, clearly signalled.

references/color.md

# Color

Color sets mood before anything is read, and it carries state, emphasis and meaning. Choose how much color the page uses first, then which colors, then build them as a system.

## Decide

1. **Inherit.** Existing brand colors and tokens win (`extend.md`). Extend their ramps; don't replace them.
2. **Strategy.** Pick one of the four below for this surface's mode.
3. **Source.** List the colors of the subject's world: its objects, places, materials, the light it is used in, and for software its interface, states, signals and output. Pick from that list, not from what websites usually look like.
4. **Light or dark.** Decide from where and when the product is used (rules below), not from taste. Light grounds, warm off-whites included, are fine when the scene suits them; dark is never a way to look different.
5. **Build.** Ramps in OKLCH, tinted neutrals, semantic colors, tokens.
6. **Look.** Render the first screen and check it as a visitor would: a calm ground, text that reads easily, and one accent the eye goes to first. If the colors fight or shout, quiet them before adding anything.

## Strategy

| Strategy | What it is | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Restrained** | Tinted neutrals carry the page; one accent marks actions and state, under roughly 10% of the area | Operate by default; Read; Persuade when the content (photos, product) brings the color |
| **Committed** | One brand hue owns large surfaces (a header field, a section, the primary surfaces) plus neutrals | Persuade; Read for a brand with a strong owned color; Operate only in chrome (sidebar, header), never behind data |
| **Full palette** | Several hues, each with a fixed role (categories, products, characters, chart series) | When the subject has real categories, or the genre is plural (children's, food, events, editorial). Every hue needs a job |
| **Drenched** | One hue floods the whole view; text and surfaces are tones of that hue | Persuade only. Not for Operate or long Read |

AVOID mixing strategies within one surface. If you can't name the strategy, the page has none.

## Rules

- **SHOULD build ramps in OKLCH.** Its lightness channel is perceptually even, so equal L steps look like equal steps across hues, and changing L keeps the hue stable, which HSL does not (HSL yellow and blue at the same "lightness" look nothing alike).
- **SHOULD step lightness, not chroma, to make a ramp**, with 9–12 steps from near-white to near-black. Reduce chroma toward both ends: very light and very dark colors can't hold high chroma inside sRGB, and out-of-gamut values get clipped or mapped by the browser, often shifting hue. Check each step is in sRGB gamut; offer wider-gamut values only inside `@media (color-gamut: p3)`.
- **SHOULD tint neutrals toward the brand hue** with very low chroma (about 0.005–0.02). Grays, borders and dark surfaces then belong to the palette. Keep the tint consistent across the whole neutral ramp.
- **SHOULD ration the accent.** It marks the primary action, current selection, focus and key data, nothing decorative. One primary action per view. If everything is accented, nothing is.
- **SHOULD derive semantic colors in the same system.** Success, warning, danger and info get their own ramps at similar lightness and chroma to the brand ramp, so they sit in the palette rather than looking pasted in. If the brand hue is close to a semantic hue (a red brand, a green brand), separate them by hue shift, lightness and an icon or label, and never use the brand color for a destructive action.
- **NEVER carry meaning by color alone.** Pair status colors with text, icons or patterns; charts get labels or markers.
- **SHOULD choose light or dark from physical context.** Dim environments, long sessions at night, media and imaging, control rooms and terminals favour dark. Bright offices, outdoors, print-adjacent and long-form reading favour light. When both are supported, follow `prefers-color-scheme` and offer a manual switch.
- **Dark mode is a second design, not an inversion:**
  - SHOULD use a tinted, near-black base, not `#000`; pure black with white text smears on many displays.
  - SHOULD show elevation by lightness: raised surfaces are lighter. Shadows barely read on dark.
  - SHOULD lower chroma of large colored areas and accents compared to light mode; saturated color on dark vibrates.
  - SHOULD keep body text slightly below full white.
  - MUST re-check every contrast pair; ratios don't survive inversion.
  - SHOULD set `color-scheme` so form controls and scrollbars match.
- **MUST meet contrast** (table below) for text in every state, including placeholders, muted text, text on images and text on every point of a gradient. Disabled controls are exempt, but must still look disabled, not invisible.
- **Gradients need a purpose:** a light source, depth, a material, a transition between two real states. When used:
  - SHOULD stay same-hue or analogous (neighbouring hues). Distant hues need an intermediate stop.
  - SHOULD interpolate in a perceptual space: `linear-gradient(in oklch, …)` keeps chroma but can swing through unexpected hues between distant colors; `in oklab` takes the straight path with no hue swing, but can dip toward gray between near-complements. The default sRGB interpolation often produces a muddy middle.
  - SHOULD check banding on large, low-contrast gradients; a subtle noise layer or more stops fixes it.
- **MUST use tokens.** Two layers: primitive ramps (`--blue-600`) and semantic roles (`--color-surface`, `--color-text-muted`, `--color-accent`, `--color-danger`, `--color-border`). Components reference roles only; themes remap roles to different primitives.

## Values

| Pair | Minimum (WCAG 2.x AA) |
|---|---|
| Body and small text | 4.5:1 |
| Large text (24px+, or 19px+ bold) | 3:1 |
| UI component boundaries, focus indicators, icons that carry meaning, chart marks | 3:1 against adjacent colors |
| Enhanced (AAA) body text | 7:1 |

| OKLCH | Range |
|---|---|
| L | 0 to 1 (0% to 100%) |
| C | 0 up to about 0.37; most sRGB colors sit under 0.25 |
| H | 0–360 degrees |
| Neutral tint chroma | about 0.005–0.02 |

Contrast ratios are computed from relative luminance, not from OKLCH L; always measure the final pair.

## Generic defaults to catch

Palette tells live in `tells.md` (purple-blue gradients, glows, untinted neutrals, the safe "tasteful" palette, glass). Also catch:

- **The framework's default palette used as the brand** → recognisable instantly → build ramps from your source colors.
- **Accent on headings, icons, links, borders and buttons at once** → no hierarchy → ration it.
- **Semantic colors at full saturation next to a muted brand** → they shout → match lightness and chroma to the system.
- **Dark mode made by inverting light mode** → wrong elevation, harsh contrast → design it per the dark-mode rules.
- **Muted gray text that fails 4.5:1** → the most common contrast failure → darken until it passes.
- **Colored shadows and glows to add "depth"** → decoration → depth from lightness and layering; glow only where light has a source in the product.

## Check

- You can name the strategy and the subject source of each hue.
- Every color in the code is a token; components use role tokens only.
- One primary accent per view; it marks action or state, not decoration.
- All text pairs meet 4.5:1 (3:1 large); UI boundaries and focus meet 3:1, in light and dark.
- Status is readable in grayscale (icon or label present).
- Neutrals carry a consistent tint; no stray pure grays.
- Dark mode: no `#000` base, raised surfaces lighter, accents less saturated, form controls themed.
- Gradients have a stated purpose, a declared interpolation space, and no muddy or banded middle.

references/composition.md

# Composition

How a page is put together: what the first screen does, what order the sections come in, and which skeleton carries them. Structure is the part of a design that two products most often share by accident; decide it, don't inherit it from habit.

## Decide

1. **What is the visitor's first question?** Usually one of: "what is this?", "does it work?", "is it for me?", "what does it cost?". The first viewport answers that one, and nothing else needs to.
2. **What must the first viewport do for this product?**
   - **Show** when the product is visual or easy to grasp on sight (tools, apps, physical goods, portfolios). The real thing, large, early.
   - **Claim** when the value is an idea the visitor must accept first (new category, service, policy). One concrete sentence, set with conviction.
   - **Set a mood** when the product is felt before it's understood (venues, fashion, music, hospitality). One real image or atmosphere, minimal text.
   - **Get to work** when the visitor already knows why they're here (docs, dashboards, search). The content or control itself, no preamble.
3. **What is the argument?** Write the sections as a list of questions the visitor asks in order, each answered by one section. If two sections answer the same question, merge them. If a question has no section, the page has a gap.
4. **Which skeleton fits that argument?** Pick from the vocabulary below, or combine two deliberately.
5. **How does it differ from the last build?** Check the variation axes.

## Page skeletons

| Skeleton | Shape | Fits when |
|---|---|---|
| **Demo-first** | Product UI or live example fills the first screen; text is a caption; sections walk through real use | The product sells itself on sight |
| **Long argument** | A single readable column of claim, evidence, objection, answer; few images | Complex or skeptical buyers; services, policy, technical depth |
| **Index** | A dense, scannable list or grid of items with filters; little intro | Catalogues, directories, templates, collections, changelogs |
| **Single statement** | One screen, one sentence, one action; maybe a short second screen | Waitlists, launches, events, personal sites |
| **Editorial** | Magazine rhythm: varied column widths, pull quotes, large images, chapters | Brands with a story and real material to show |
| **Comparison-led** | Opens with the choice the visitor is making (plans, before/after, us vs the old way) | Pricing pages, migrations, alternatives to an incumbent |
| **Timeline** | Sections ordered by time or process step, visibly sequenced | Processes, histories, onboarding, how something is made |
| **Document** | Looks like a well-set document: headings, numbered sections, footnotes, a contents list | Technical, legal, research or manifesto-like products |
| **Gallery-led** | Images carry the page; text is labels and captions | Photography, architecture, products bought on looks |
| **Tool-as-page** | The page is a working calculator, converter or demo; explanation sits below | Utilities, APIs, anything that can be tried without signing up |

## Variation axes

In New world work, consecutive builds SHOULD differ on at least two of these (the last build is whatever you can see: earlier in the conversation or `.gradientdeck/decisions.md`). Name the two in your design note. In Extend and New surface, inherit instead.

- **First viewport:** show, claim, mood, get to work; full-height vs partial; centered vs asymmetric.
- **Navigation:** top bar, side rail, inline contents list, minimal (logo + one action), none.
- **Section rhythm:** uniform blocks, alternating dense/sparse, one long flow, chapters with breaks.
- **Grid:** single column, two unequal columns, multi-column editorial, full-bleed with insets.
- **Image role:** evidence, atmosphere, explanation, none (see `imagery.md`).
- **Footer:** minimal line, sitemap, closing statement, contact block, none.

## Rules

- SHOULD let every section answer one question, and do one of four jobs: **explain** (what it is, how it works), **prove** (evidence for a claim), **deepen** (detail for people already convinced) or **convert** (the next step). A section that does none of these is cut, however good it looks.
- SHOULD vary section weight to match importance. The most persuasive section gets the most space; supporting detail gets less.
- SHOULD pass the **brand test** in Persuade mode: hide the logo and nav, then look at the first viewport. If it could belong to another company in the same category, the product's identity isn't in it yet; change the content or structure, not the decoration.
- AVOID filling the first viewport to exactly 100vh by default. Let the next section peek in when the page continues, so scrolling feels invited.
- SHOULD place proof next to the claim it supports, not in a separate "testimonials" band. NEVER invent it (see `SKILL.md`).
- SHOULD keep the page as short as the argument. Stop when the questions run out.

### Navigation

- SHOULD size the nav to the site: a five-page site needs no mega-menu; a single page may need only a logo and one action.
- MUST keep navigation reachable by keyboard, with the current page marked by more than color (see `accessibility.md`).
- SHOULD make sticky headers short and only sticky when the page is long enough to need them.
- On mobile, SHOULD keep the primary action visible outside the menu (see `responsive.md`).

### Calls to action

- SHOULD have one primary action per page, repeated where the argument resolves (after the key evidence and at the end), not after every section.
- SHOULD name the actual action (see `copy.md`). One secondary action at most beside it, visibly lower in weight.
- AVOID a closing full-width "Ready to get started?" band by default. End on the strongest evidence or a direct next step.

### Footers

- SHOULD match the footer to what visitors look for at the end: legal and contact for most sites, a sitemap only when there are enough pages to need one.
- AVOID four equal link columns, a newsletter box and social icons as the reflex footer.

## By mode

- **Persuade:** everything above applies. Structure is a primary place to be specific.
- **Operate:** follow app-shell conventions. Navigation in a side rail or top bar, consistent across screens; page title and primary action top of content; content fills the remaining space. Don't invent layouts per screen. See `apps-and-data.md`.
- **Read:** a reading column of 45–75 characters, generous margins, a contents list for long pages (sticky in the margin on wide screens), headings that work as an outline. Character goes in the margins, header and type, not in the column. See `typography.md`.
- **Extend / New surface:** inherit the existing nav, footer and section patterns. Decide only the order and skeleton of the new page (see `extend.md`).

## Generic defaults to catch

- **The default skeleton** (hero, three cards, testimonial, CTA band, footer) → no decision behind the order → write the visitor's questions, then choose a skeleton from the table.
- **Centered full-height hero with headline, subline, two buttons** → see `tells.md` → decide show / claim / mood / get to work first.
- **Every section the same height, padding and layout** → no hierarchy across the page → vary weight by importance.
- **Alternating image-left / image-right rows for every feature** → zig-zag filler → group features by the question they answer; show the few that matter.
- **Same nav and footer on every build** → the frame becomes a signature → choose them along with the skeleton.

## Check

- The first viewport answers one named visitor question, and you can say which.
- Each section maps to one question and one job (explain, prove, deepen, convert); no two answer the same one.
- Persuade: with logo and nav hidden, the first viewport still couldn't belong to a competitor.
- The skeleton is named in the design note, with the two variation axes that differ from the last build.
- One primary action, with a specific label, placed where the argument resolves.
- Nav and footer are sized to the site, keyboard-reachable, with current page marked.
- Operate screens share one shell; Read pages keep the column at 45–75 characters.

references/copy.md

# Copy

Words are part of the interface. They decide whether a page says something only this product could say, and whether people know what will happen when they act. Write the copy before you style it; layout built around placeholder text breaks when real words arrive.

## Decide

1. **Who reads this, and what do they already know?** A tax adviser, a teenager and an on-call engineer need different vocabulary, sentence length and warmth. Write down the reader in one line.
2. **What voice fits that reader and this product?** Pick it from the audience and the subject, not from the habit of sounding like a friendly startup. A clinical product may be precise and calm; a hobby tool may be loose. Inherit an existing voice guide or the tone of existing screens if there is one.
3. **What is the one thing this text must get across?** One message per headline, one action per button.
4. **What words do users actually use?** Take nouns from the product's domain and the codebase (the real feature names, the real objects), not from marketing synonyms.

## Rules

### Headlines and subcopy (mostly Persuade)

- SHOULD state the specific value: what the product does, for whom, with what result. **Test:** could a competitor's site use this headline unchanged? If yes, rewrite it.
- SHOULD put the concrete noun in the headline ("Payroll for restaurants with tipped staff"), not an abstract promise ("Work smarter").
- Subcopy SHOULD add information the headline doesn't have: how it works, who it's for, what it replaces. If it restates the headline in more words, cut it.
- AVOID headlines that need the image beside them to make sense.

### Calls to action

- SHOULD name the action and its object: "Create invoice", "Book a demo", "Download the report (PDF, 2 MB)". The label says what happens on click.
- SHOULD keep the same verb through a flow: a button labelled "Send invite" leads to a dialog titled "Send invite" and a confirmation "Invite sent".
- AVOID two buttons with equal weight and vague labels ("Get started" / "Learn more"). If there are two, the second names a different action.

### States and tense

- Action labels are imperative; results are past tense: "Publish" → "Publishing…" → "Published". "Save" → "Saved 2 min ago".
- Toggles and status labels describe the current state, not the action, unless they are buttons. A switch reads "Notifications", not "Turn on notifications".
- Use the ellipsis on a label only when the action opens a step that asks for more input ("Rename…").

### Errors

- MUST say what happened, why if known, and what to do next, in that order: "Card declined. Your bank refused the charge. Try another card or contact your bank."
- SHOULD NOT apologise by reflex or blame the user ("You entered an invalid date"). State the fact: "Use a date after 1 Jan 2026."
- NEVER show an error code alone. A code may follow the message for support ("Reference: 4F2A").
- Field errors sit next to the field and name the field. Form-level errors summarise and link to each field (see `accessibility.md`).
- Keep the user's input. An error never clears what they typed.

### Empty states

- SHOULD tell people why it's empty and what to do next, with the action right there: "No invoices yet. Create one, or import from a spreadsheet."
- Distinguish first-use empty, filtered-to-nothing ("No results for 'acme'. Clear filters") and cleared-out ("All caught up"). Each needs different words.

### Microcopy

- Button labels: one to three words, verb first, sentence case.
- Field labels: a noun, visible, above or beside the field. Placeholder text is not a label (`interaction.md`).
- Helper text says the constraint before the error does ("At least 12 characters").
- Tooltips add information; they never hold the only copy of something essential, and never repeat the visible label.
- Pick one case style for UI labels (sentence case is easiest to read) and keep it everywhere.

### Numbers, units and dates

- SHOULD format with the user's locale (thousands separators, decimal mark, currency position). Use the platform's number and date formatters, not string concatenation.
- Keep a number and its unit together with a non-breaking space ("12 GB"), and use the same unit throughout a view.
- Round to the precision people act on. "4.2k" in a summary; the exact figure in the detail or on hover.
- Use unambiguous dates ("3 Apr 2026", not "03/04/26"). Relative time ("5 min ago") for recent events, with the absolute timestamp available on hover or focus.
- Ranges use an en dash ("10–20"); negative numbers use a real minus sign or a clear "−" in data.

### Honesty

- NEVER invent claims, metrics, customer names, quotes or ratings (SKILL.md rule).
- NEVER write urgency or scarcity that isn't true ("Only 2 left", countdown timers on evergreen offers).
- Facts and demo content differ. Demo content (a sample entry, a name in a product demo, example data) is authored at full quality and labelled as an example. Facts (dates, prices, contacts) are written around instead of printed as gaps. No date yet: "New dates go out to the list first". No price: "Ask for a quote". No email: the contact form or the channel the user did give. If a sentence can't stand without the fact, cut the sentence. Mark the spot with an HTML comment and list it in your report. No bracketed placeholders, "TBD" or lorem ipsum in visible text.

### Length and readability

- Cut every word that doesn't change the meaning. "In order to" → "to"; "Click here to download" → "Download".
- Front-load: the key word goes first in headings, list items and labels, because people scan the first two words.
- SHOULD aim for sentences under about 20 words in UI text, and one idea per sentence.
- Use plain words over jargon unless the audience shares the jargon. Developer tools can say "webhook"; a consumer app shouldn't.

### Inclusive language

- Address people directly ("you"); avoid gendered defaults, idioms and culture-bound jokes that won't translate.
- Describe what to do, not how to do it physically: "Select", not "Click" or "Tap", when it could be either.
- Leave room for translation: allow labels to grow 30–40% without breaking the layout.

## Generic defaults to catch

The general cadence tells (hype words, "not just X but Y", triplets, em-dash rhythm, rhetorical headlines) are listed in `tells.md`. Specific to copy:

- **Headline that fits any product** ("Build faster", "The platform for modern teams") → no information → name the user, the job and the outcome.
- **"Oops! Something went wrong"** → cute and useless → what happened, why, what to do.
- **"No data"** as an empty state → a dead end → why it's empty plus the next action.
- **"Submit", "OK", "Yes"** as button labels → the user has to read the question again → name the action ("Delete 3 files").
- **Exclamation marks on routine success** ("Saved!") → shouting → plain past tense.
- **Feature lists of abstract nouns** ("Speed. Security. Scale.") → says nothing → one concrete sentence per feature, or show it.
- **Every heading the same length and shape** → reads generated → let headings vary with what they need to say.

## Check

- [ ] The headline would not fit a competitor unchanged.
- [ ] Subcopy adds a fact the headline doesn't contain.
- [ ] Every button names its action; no "Submit", "OK" or lone "Learn more".
- [ ] States move imperative → progressive → past ("Save" → "Saving…" → "Saved").
- [ ] Every error says what happened and what to do, without a bare code or blame.
- [ ] Every empty state offers a next action; filtered-empty offers "Clear filters".
- [ ] Numbers and dates are locale-formatted, units consistent, dates unambiguous.
- [ ] No invented claims; missing facts are written around or cut, never shown as placeholders, and listed in the report.
- [ ] One case style for labels; no placeholder used as a label.
- [ ] No sentence survives that loses nothing when deleted.

references/craft.md

# Craft

The floor every page must clear, whatever its direction. Read this immediately before writing or editing UI code, including small changes. The direction and the brand decide what the page is; this file decides whether it's well made. A brand's or user's explicit choice overrides a line here; your own habit doesn't.

Each line is a check on the rendered result, not an intention. Check them on your screenshots at 1440 and 390, all in one pass. With every line met, spend everything else on the committed idea; when torn between refined and committed, commit.

## Type

- SHOULD choose the body face first: easy to read at 16px, with regular, bold and italic. Then a headline face that differs from it in one clear way (structure, width or texture) and suits the tone. Two families at most; a third only for code or figures. In Persuade work, a face on the overused list in `tells.md` needs a reason in the plan no other face meets.
- AVOID condensed or monospace faces as the page's voice. Monospace is for code, data and values; condensed is for tight data or a single short display line.
- AVOID all-caps headings longer than three or four words. Capitals slow reading and turn loud at size.
- SHOULD size the largest heading to the message: at 1440 it stays under about 6rem and wraps to at most four lines. If it's bigger, the page is shouting.
- SHOULD keep a clear scale: each heading level differs from the next by size, and by weight where useful. Body text at least 16px (13–14px only in dense Operate UI), running text 45–75 characters per line.

## Color

- SHOULD name the strategy before choosing colors (restrained, committed, full palette, drenched; `color.md`) and keep to it across the page.
- SHOULD give the page one accent, used for the main action, the current selection and states. If three things compete for the eye, quiet two of them.
- SHOULD tint neutrals slightly toward the palette; grays, borders and dark surfaces belong to it. Secondary text on color is tinted from that color, never plain gray.
- SHOULD choose light or dark from where the page is used (`color.md`), never to look different.
- MUST meet contrast: 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for large text, including muted text and text on color.

## Space, boxes and borders

- SHOULD group with space and alignment first. A border, fill or shadow marks a real boundary, never decoration.
- AVOID boxes inside boxes. Inside a section, at most one level of bordered or filled container; content inside it is separated by space or a single rule. The exception is the product's own interface shown working: its panels nest as the real product's do.
- AVOID borders and fills on every element at once. Pick one way to separate surfaces and use it consistently (`space-and-layout.md`).
- SHOULD make the space between groups clearly larger than the space within them, about 1.5–2×, and leave a section room to breathe. Cramped reads cheap; space is not waste.
- SHOULD keep one container width and shared edges, so sections line up.

## Finish values

Defaults for the details models leave at browser settings. The world or brand overrides any of them on purpose.

| Detail | Default |
|---|---|
| Corners | One radius family. Cards and panels about 8–16px, controls the same or smaller, full pills only for small controls and tags |
| Shadows | An offset and a soft blur (blur at least twice the offset), tinted toward the ground. Never a zero-offset colored halo. One elevation method: border or shadow, not both |
| Borders | 1px. On dark grounds a hairline a few steps lighter than the surface |
| Space around headings | About twice as much space above a heading as below it |
| Line height | Display 1.0–1.15, headings 1.15–1.3, body 1.5–1.7 |
| Display tracking | −0.01 to −0.03em for large sizes; never tighter than −0.04em. Small caps and labels get slight positive tracking |
| Section spacing (Persuade) | About 96–160px between sections at 1440, 56–96px at 390 |
| Buttons | Horizontal padding about 1.5–2× the vertical; at least 44px tall on touch |
| Weights | Two or three per family, each with a job |

## Web material and finish

The web has its own materials: light, geometry, motion and layered surfaces. They are as valid as paper or metal when they come from what the product does.

- SHOULD build the technique the direction names (canvas, SVG geometry, animated lines, a shader, view transitions), not a static picture of it. Drive it from the product's behaviour or data. Its first frame reads on its own; reduced motion shows that frame still.
- SHOULD draw with exact geometry: crisp shapes, diagrams, lines and grids you can specify. AVOID sketchy SVG scenes that imitate illustration, and grids or stripes with nothing measured under them.
- SHOULD give light one source and a falloff: a gradient or glow starts where something happens (the output, the active state) and fades. Two light sources compete.
- SHOULD show depth on dark grounds by lightness: each raised surface a step lighter.
- SHOULD spend motion on one authored moment and on state changes: 150–300ms, ease-out, from an already visible state. Blur, mask and clip-path are material too, not just fades.
- SHOULD theme what the browser draws: text selection, caret, scrollbars, focus ring, link underline offset, and tabular figures in numbers that line up. It's the cheapest sign a page was built, not assembled.

## Refuse

Defaults that mark a page as generated. The brief's own words can earn any of them back; your habit can't.

- A small spaced-out label (eyebrow) above headings. The heading carries itself.
- A row of same-size cards, each an icon tile, a title and two lines, as the page's structure.
- Section numbers (01 / 02 / 03) on content that isn't a sequence.
- Gradient text; glass and blur as decoration; a thick colored border on one side of cards.
- Monospace as "technical" costume; emoji or Unicode symbols as icons.
- Sketch-style SVG scenes standing in for real illustration or a photograph.
- A page about a place, food, a craft or an event with no photograph of it.

## By mode

- **Persuade: the visitor gets it, wants it and acts.** One idea owns the page, and one bold move is spent in one place (a color field, a scale jump, the page's object, the signature moment); around it, things stay calm so the move reads. Pace the scroll: vary density, scale, imagery and quiet inside one system; a dense passage earns a quiet one, no two neighbouring sections share a shape, and the page ends on a real close with the action in working form.
- **Operate: the task gets done fast, every day.** Standard layout and controls (`apps-and-data.md`). One family, or one plus a face for figures. Restrained palette: neutrals carry the screen, the accent marks actions, selection and state only. Rows and tables over cards; a card holds one thing. Character lives in precise details: type, palette, states and one small signature, never the layout. No illustrations in the working area.
- **Read: the reader understands and stays.** The column stays calm: 60–75 characters, body 16–20px, generous leading. The usual docs frame (sidebar, on-page contents) stays. Character lives in the frame, the headings and the imagery, never in the text column.

## Verify before you finish

- At 390, nothing is cramped: no box inside a box, tap targets at least 44px, text not squeezed into narrow columns.
- The largest heading is under about 6rem at 1440 and no more than four lines.
- Two font families at most (plus one for code or figures), each with a job you can name.
- One accent leads the eye; nothing else shouts.
- Every border or box marks a real boundary; corners, shadows and spacing follow the finish values or a stated reason.
- Neighbouring sections differ in shape and density, and the page ends on a real close.
- Any glow, gradient or animated visual has a source in the product, and the product's interface, if shown, works.
- Selection, focus and scrollbars belong to the palette. Nothing from the Refuse list is left.

references/design-md.md

# DESIGN.md

The file that records a product's design system so the next task, and the next agent, inherits it instead of reinventing it. Also covers the two small files beside it: `.gradientdeck/decisions.md` and `.gradientdeck/config.json`.

## The format

`DESIGN.md` sits at the project root. It has two parts:

1. **YAML frontmatter of tokens.** Groups: `colors`, `typography`, `rounded`, `spacing`, and `components`. Components reference other tokens with `{path.to.token}` instead of repeating values, so a change in one place carries through.
2. **Prose sections**, in this order: Overview, Colors, Typography, Layout, Elevation & Depth, Shapes, Components, Do's and Don'ts.

**Tokens are normative; prose explains why.** If the two disagree, the tokens win and the prose is out of date: fix it. Prose says what each role is for, when to use it, and what was rejected, so a later agent can extend the system without guessing.

## Rules

- MUST treat an existing `DESIGN.md` as authority over your own taste (SKILL.md inputs). Change it only when the user asks, or when a decision you've made with them supersedes it, and say so in your report.
- SHOULD write `DESIGN.md` **after the first build** in New world work, not before. A rulebook written before anything exists gets defended against the real page; one written after records what survived. Seed it from the page's plan in `.gradientdeck/pages/` (`direction.md`).
- SHOULD write it for existing code via the `extract` command (`extend.md`), recording the de facto system, not an idealised one.
- SHOULD name tokens by role (`ink`, `surface`, `accent`, `danger`), not by appearance (`blue-500`, `dark-grey`). Raw scales can exist beneath roles; components reference roles.
- SHOULD record provenance for each token group or token: `decided` (chosen in direction work, with the reason in prose) or `extracted` (found in code, with source and confidence).
- SHOULD record the mode for each main route or route group (Persuade, Operate, Read), so the next task knows how much expression it may use.
- SHOULD keep it current: when a build adds or changes a token or component on purpose, update `DESIGN.md` in the same change.
- AVOID prose that restates values ("the accent is a blue"). Explain the role and the reason.
- AVOID a Do's and Don'ts list of generic advice. Each line should be specific to this system and checkable ("Accent fills only the primary action per view", not "use colour wisely").
- Don't put design notes, scores or signatures in the product's code or comments; they belong here or in the decisions log (SKILL.md).

## Example skeleton

Placeholders only. Replace every name and value with what the product actually uses.

```markdown
---
provenance: decided            # or: extracted (from <files>)
modes:
  "/": persuade
  "/app/*": operate
  "/docs/*": read
colors:
  ink: "<value>"               # primary text
  ink-muted: "<value>"         # secondary text, meets 4.5:1 on surface
  surface: "<value>"
  surface-raised: "<value>"
  accent: "<value>"
  danger: "<value>"
typography:
  display: { family: "<family>", weight: <n>, tracking: "<value>" }
  body: { family: "<family>", size: "<value>", leading: <n> }
  data: { family: "<family>", features: "tabular-nums" }
  scale: ["<step>", "<step>", "<step>", "<step>"]
rounded:
  sm: "<value>"
  md: "<value>"
spacing:
  scale: ["<step>", "<step>", "<step>", "<step>", "<step>"]
components:
  button-primary:
    background: "{colors.accent}"
    text: "{colors.surface}"
    radius: "{rounded.sm}"
    padding: "{spacing.scale.1} {spacing.scale.3}"
  card:
    background: "{colors.surface-raised}"
    radius: "{rounded.md}"
---

## Overview
What the product is, who uses it, the core idea in one sentence, the one bold move.

## Colors
Each role and when it's used. Strategy. Contrast pairs checked. What was rejected.

## Typography
Each role and where its voice comes from. Scale logic. Line length.

## Layout
Grid, containers, spacing rhythm, density per mode.

## Elevation & Depth
How layers are separated (surface steps, borders, shadows) and the limits.

## Shapes
Radii and why; icon style.

## Components
Each component, its variants, its states, and the tokens it uses.

## Do's and Don'ts
- Do: <specific, checkable rule for this system>
- Don't: <specific thing that breaks this system>
```

For extracted files, add a source and confidence comment to each token (`# from tokens.css --text-primary, high` or `# inferred from usage, 41 occurrences, medium`) and an "Open questions" list after Do's and Don'ts for drift the user should resolve.

## `.gradientdeck/decisions.md`

A log of design decisions that should hold next time. One dated line each, with the reason:

```
2026-03-02  Tables stay at 13px body on /app: users scan hundreds of rows; density over comfort.
2026-03-09  No illustrations on marketing pages: rejected as interchangeable; product screenshots only.
```

- SHOULD add a line whenever the user settles a question, or you make a choice that a later task might otherwise reverse.
- SHOULD append, never rewrite history. A reversed decision gets a new dated line that says what it supersedes.
- Ratified decisions are not findings: `review.md` doesn't report them, unless one now causes a P0 (an accessibility or honesty failure), which always gets reported.

## `.gradientdeck/pages/<page>.md`

The plan for one New world page, saved by the direction roll and filled in by you (`direction.md`). It is a snapshot, not a log: rolling that page again replaces the whole file, carrying over only the job, the action and the worlds already dealt.

- SHOULD read it before changing that page later, as the page's intent. Changing the page's direction means a new roll, not editing the plan to match drift.
- Commit it with `decisions.md`; it is how the next agent knows why the page looks the way it does.
- NEVER copy it into the page, and keep `.gradientdeck/` out of what gets deployed if the site is served from the project folder.

## `.gradientdeck/config.json`

Project settings for the skill. Its main job is scoped ignores: telling reviews to skip a check where the project has a reason.

```json
{
  "ignore": [
    {
      "rule": "<check or tell name>",
      "scope": "<route, file glob or selector>",
      "reason": "<why this is right for this product>"
    }
  ]
}
```

- Every ignore is scoped to a route, file pattern or selector. A global ignore turns a check off for work nobody has looked at yet.
- Every ignore carries a reason. Treat an ignore with no scope or no reason as absent.
- NEVER accept an ignore for the accessibility floor or for invented proof. Those can't be configured away.

## Check

- Frontmatter parses as YAML; every `{reference}` resolves to a defined token.
- Prose sections are present and in order.
- Every token has provenance; extracted tokens have source and confidence.
- Each main route has a mode.
- Decisions are dated, one line each, with a reason.
- Every ignore in config has a scope and a reason, and none touches accessibility or honesty.

references/direction.md

# Direction

How to choose a visual direction for New world work: greenfield builds and redesigns. **In New world, this is required before any code.** Skip it in Extend and New surface: the existing system is the direction (`extend.md`).

Left alone, a model builds its top-ranked idea, the one every other run would build too. So you write the candidates, a roll picks one, and dealt worlds push it further.

## 1. Ground in the subject

One line each:
- **Audience:** who arrives, what they already know, what they're afraid of.
- **Job:** the one thing a visitor must understand or do.
- **Action:** the control that does the job, in working form on the first screen (the order form, the install command, the booking slot, the call button). Not a link to it.
- **Scene:** where they are and what's around them when this matters (a 6am queue, a late-night deploy, a tax deadline).
- **Vocabulary:** the words users actually say. Not marketing words.

Then list 8–12 things only this subject has: objects, processes, units, rituals, documents, constraints. "Fast" and "easy" don't count.

## 2. Name the rut

Describe the page this category always ships (palette, type, first screen, imagery) and its predictable opposite (soft and friendly becomes stark and brutal). Rule out both. The test: if someone could guess your look from the category alone, or from the category plus what you avoided, you're still in the rut. Dodging the dark software look by dressing a software product as an old paper object is the predictable opposite, not an escape. A look from `tells.md` is fine when this product's facts reshape it.

## 3. Write seven candidates

Seven concrete worlds the audience knows by heart that could lend the page its materials. Their world includes what they read on screens, not only what they hold: a printed object, a place, a ritual, signage, a broadcast, a craft, a game, and also an interface they admire, a notation, a data graphic, an identity program, a named school of design. A nameable system is as concrete as an object; a mood ("clean", "premium") is not.
- Cover at least three material families (paper and print; metal and machinery; textile; built space and signage; food and packaging; screen and broadcast; sport and play; interface and notation; light, signal and motion).
- At most one comes from the tools the audience operates for this job (a terminal for a developer tool, flour sacks for a bakery). Interfaces and graphics they admire elsewhere don't count as that one. At most one reads the product's name literally.
- Give each one line: its ground color, two or three main colors, where its type comes from, and the one thing it does that nothing else on the list does.
- Give each a reason: how it carries the job or the action, and where the product is seen working on its first screen (which part becomes the action, which state shows the product's facts). Colors and type are not a reason.
- Every candidate must already be a page you could finish well, since the roll may land on any of your top three. One that couldn't is replaced before the roll, never rescued by it.

Rank them by how strongly the audience would recognise each as theirs.

## 4. Roll

Run the roll from the project folder:

```
node <skill folder>/scripts/roll.mjs --page index --job "<job>" --action "<action>"
  --candidates "<world name>: <reason and first screen> | ..." --mode persuade
  --photos "<thing to show> | <thing to show>"
```

Pass your seven, best first, each with its reason after a colon. `--page` names the page (`index`, `pricing`). Use `--mode operate` or `--mode read` for those surfaces. `--photos` names what its photographs show (or `none: <reason>`). Its output is binding: the candidate to build, worlds to weigh against it, this mode's rules, matching photographs, and the plan file (section 6). Without Node, build your third-ranked candidate with no dealt worlds, write the plan file yourself, and say so.

## 5. Weigh the dealt worlds

In Operate mode the roll deals no worlds; skip this step. Otherwise, follow the roll's instructions. In short: imagine the product built in each world's system, judge it against your assigned candidate on two things only (does the audience recognise it, is the product clearer), and write a verdict for each in the plan file. A world that wins both becomes the build. Every other world lends one discipline from its system to your direction, never a color, typeface or ornament.

## 6. Fill the plan

The roll saves `.gradientdeck/pages/<page>.md` in the project: the roll's key and pick, the job, the action, your ranked list, and blanks to fill before code: thesis, first screen, type and color, the page's own system, the story section by section, the signature moment, the example content you authored, and one verdict per dealt world. Its Finish line says when the page is done. Rolling the page again replaces it; job, action and dealt worlds carry over. Later edits read it as the page's intent.

The first screen is described spatially, as if to someone drawing it. Copy beside a picture is fine when the picture is this product's own thing, shown working (the order docket, the marked-up proof, the editor mid-task); a generic card or a centred headline over cards is not. When the world is an object, the page is built as that object. When it's an interface, a notation or a system of light and motion, the page is built around the product's own interface shown working, and the world sets its type, surfaces, how states change and one signature visual. The world carries every section, not just the first: a section that reads as ordinary docs, steps or a card grid in the world's colors has dropped it.

## 7. Present, build, re-roll

- **If you can ask the user,** follow the roll's PRESENT step: show the assigned direction committed, your pick if allowed, any world that won or came close, and the exits (bolder, safer, the category standard). Build what they choose.
- **If you can't ask,** build the assigned direction. End your report with one line offering a bolder or safer re-roll.
- **Before you finish,** render the page and run the roll's `check` command; fix what it lists as part of the taste-test (SKILL.md).
- **When the user asks to re-roll,** run the script again for the same page with `--register bolder` (a dealt world is built outright) or `--register safer` (one of your top three, executed straight). Worlds already dealt don't come back. If they ask for the standard, build the category canon at full craft, measured against two or three real products they'd name. If they say they prefer one register for this product, add a dated line to `.gradientdeck/decisions.md`.

## Committing

- Build the direction you were given, not a safer reading of it. When torn between refined and committed, commit.
- The world shows across the page (its object, its structure, its colors), not as one sticker on a generic page. The ground can still be light and quiet.
- Name a color strategy: restrained, committed (one saturated color over a third of the page), full palette, or drenched. Bold usually means committed or drenched.
- Pick type and color by the procedures in `typography.md` and `color.md`, which end in looking at a render. A face on the overused list in `tells.md` needs a written reason no other face meets; the subject's cliche is not one. A dark or loud palette chosen only to look different is a new default, not a fix.
- Missing content never shrinks the idea or drops a section. Author demonstration content (a demo's entries and data, sample names, example images) at full quality and label it as an example; dropping a bold idea because its demo content doesn't exist yet is timidity, not honesty. Claims and product facts are still never invented (SKILL.md).

## Mode limits

| Mode | The direction may set | It leaves alone |
|---|---|---|
| Persuade | Everything: structure, type, color, imagery, one expressive motion moment | Accessibility floor, honesty |
| Read | Type pairing, color, the frame around the reading column, imagery | The column itself (`typography.md`) |
| Operate | Type, palette, density, one signature detail | Layout conventions, controls, navigation (`apps-and-data.md`) |

A product that spans modes gets one direction that steps down: palette roles, type voice and the signature carry through; the structural ideas and expressive motion drop away.

## Check

- The rut and its opposite are named; seven candidates span three material families, each with a reason that carries the job and names its first screen.
- The plan file is filled, and the built candidate is the one the roll named, unless a factual reason is written in it.
- The action sits on the first screen in working form.
- Every section is in the world, not only the first screen.
- Each dealt world has a verdict, and the raises are disciplines, not clothes.
- The first screen shows this product's own thing, not a generic card or a centred headline over cards.
- Type and color were chosen on a render: the pairing beat another one, and the text reads easily at both widths.
- Nothing requires invented proof or product facts.

references/extend.md

# Extend

How to work inside an existing codebase: Extend (adding to a look that already exists) and New surface (a new kind of page in that look). The existing system is the authority (`principles.md`, SKILL.md inputs). Your job is to make new work indistinguishable from the best existing work, not to improve the system while nobody's looking.

## Decide

Inventory before you write a line. Spend the time; it's cheaper than undoing a drifted page.

1. **Find the tokens.** Look, in roughly this order:
   - `DESIGN.md` and `.gradientdeck/decisions.md` (`design-md.md`).
   - Tailwind v4 `@theme` blocks in CSS, or `tailwind.config.*` (`theme.extend`).
   - CSS custom properties on `:root`, `[data-theme]` or `.dark`.
   - CSS-in-JS theme objects (a `theme.ts`, a styled-system or emotion theme provider).
   - Design-token JSON or YAML (a `tokens/` folder, a build step that emits CSS variables).
2. **Find the components.** A `components/` or `ui/` folder, a `components.json` (copied-in primitives), a component-library theme (MUI, Chakra or similar `createTheme`/`extendTheme`), Storybook stories if present. Note which components exist, their variants and their props.
3. **Find the nearest sibling.** The existing page most similar to what you're building (same mode, similar content). It is your template for spacing, heading levels, section rhythm, container widths and how components are combined.
4. **Measure what's used, not just what's declared.** Search the code for actual values: spacing classes or values, radii, font sizes, weights, colours, shadows. Count frequency. The de facto scale is the set of values used often; a declared token nobody uses is not part of the system. Note outliers and drift (near-duplicate greys, a stray radius), but don't "fix" them unless asked.
5. **Note conventions.** File layout, component naming, class style (utility classes, CSS modules, styled components), how variants are expressed, how icons are imported, how copy is written (sentence case or title case, tone).

## Pre-flight contract

Before building, state this in your design note (it replaces the direction for Extend and New surface):

```
Situation: Extend | New surface    Mode: <...>
Template: <nearest sibling page/file>
Reusing: <tokens, components, patterns>
New: <each new token/component/variant, and why nothing existing fits>
Not touching: <files, global styles, shared components you'll leave alone>
Flags: <existing problems noticed, reported separately>
```

## Rules

- MUST use existing tokens. Semantic tokens (text, surface, accent, border) before raw scale steps; never raw values. If no token fits, add one to the token source on purpose and list it under New.
- MUST keep global CSS append-only. Don't edit or reorder existing global rules, resets or base styles; add scoped rules after them.
- MUST NOT add a dependency (UI library, icon set, font, animation library) without asking.
- SHOULD reach for, in this order: an existing component as-is → a composition of existing components → an existing variant → a new variant on an existing component → a new component. Overrides (one-off class or style props fighting the component) come last and need a reason.
- SHOULD match the sibling's structure: same container, same heading scale, same section spacing, same way of handling empty and loading states.
- SHOULD match conventions exactly: file names, export style, prop names, class ordering, copy tone. New code should look like the same team wrote it.
- SHOULD place any new component where existing ones live, built the way they're built.
- AVOID importing your own taste. The generic defaults in `tells.md` still apply to what you add, but if the existing system already uses one of them, it's the system: match it and mention it in Flags if it hurts.
- AVOID "while I'm here" fixes. Drift, inconsistent spacing, weak contrast or an outdated pattern in existing code go in Flags, not in the diff, unless the user asked for cleanup.
- NEVER ship an accessibility failure because the existing system has it. If inheriting a token would fail contrast or focus visibility, fix it locally for your work, and flag the source.

## New surface

The look is inherited; only structure is yours.

- Inherit tokens, components and voice completely, exactly as in Extend.
- Decide the structure for this new kind of page using `composition.md` (and `apps-and-data.md` for Operate surfaces). The sibling still sets container widths, spacing rhythm and heading levels even if its content is different.
- If the page genuinely needs something the system lacks (a pricing table, a comparison grid, a docs sidebar), build it from existing tokens and the closest existing component's anatomy. List it under New.
- Don't introduce a second visual language for the new page. If it needs more expression (a first marketing page in an app-only codebase), raise the expression through layout and content, not new colours or fonts, and say so in the note. If the user wants a new look, that's New world: load `direction.md`.

## The `extract` command

Write `DESIGN.md` from the code, in the format in `design-md.md`.

1. Run steps 1–5 above.
2. Record tokens as they're used: the de facto scale, not every declared value. Map raw values to semantic roles where usage makes the role clear (the colour on every body paragraph is the text colour).
3. Mark provenance and confidence for each token: where it came from (file and token name, or "inferred from usage, N occurrences") and high / medium / low confidence. Low means the role is a guess.
4. Write the prose sections from what the code does, not from what you'd prefer. Put drift and conflicts in a short "Open questions" list at the end, for the user to decide.
5. Note the mode for each main route (marketing pages Persuade, app routes Operate, docs Read).
6. Don't change any code during `extract`.

## Generic defaults to catch

- **A new button or card that duplicates an existing one** → the system forks → search for the component first; extend with a variant.
- **Raw values in new code** (`#3b4252`, `13px`, `rounded-[7px]`) → instant drift → map to the nearest token or add one deliberately.
- **A new page that's "better" than its siblings** (different spacing, new font size, new shadow) → reads as a different product → match the sibling, flag what you'd change.
- **A quiet global refactor** (renamed tokens, changed base font size) inside a feature change → breaks pages you didn't look at → separate change, with permission.
- **Fresh decoration on an inherited page** (a gradient section, a glow) → your taste overriding theirs → only if the system already does it.

## Check

- Every colour, size, radius, shadow and spacing value in the diff references a token.
- No new dependency; global CSS changes are additions only.
- Each new component, variant or token is listed with a reason.
- Side by side with the sibling at 1440 and 390, the new page looks like the same product.
- Existing problems are reported in Flags, not silently changed.
- After `extract`: every token in `DESIGN.md` has a source and a confidence.

references/imagery.md

# Imagery

Photographs, screenshots, illustration, icons and logos. Images are the fastest way to make a page specific, and the fastest way to make it interchangeable. Decide what an image is for before choosing one.

## Decide

1. **What role does this image play?**
   - **Evidence:** proves something real (the product's UI, the actual dish, the finished building).
   - **Atmosphere:** sets the feeling of the place or product.
   - **Explanation:** shows how something works (a diagram, an annotated screenshot).
   - **Identity:** says who this is (a founder portrait, the workshop, the logo).
   If it plays none of these, it's filler. Cut it.
2. **What real material exists?** Ask the user once whether they have photos of their own, and check the codebase. Theirs win every slot.
3. **If they have none:** photographs of the subject from the skill's library: `node <skill folder>/scripts/roll.mjs photos "<subject>"` prints matches with ready image code and credits (in New world, the roll's `--photos` prints them). For software, the product's own interface built in HTML leads, and photos set the scene. Type alone only when the page is about words. Drawings are for diagrams and icons, never in a photo's place.
4. **What single treatment will every image share?** One from the roll's list (natural, warm, muted, mono, tint, duotone), chosen to sit in the palette, plus one set of crops, frames and corners.

## Rules

### Real first

- SHOULD use real product screenshots for software: current UI, crisp at 2x, with realistic data that fits the product (real-looking names, plausible values, no lorem ipsum). Crop to the part that makes the point rather than shrinking the whole screen.
- SHOULD use real photography of the actual subject (the place, the people who work there, the object) over generic stock.
- SHOULD prefer a photograph of the actual subject to both a generic image and no image. A page about a place, food, a craft or an event with no photograph reads as a template; a page with off-subject stock reads as filler. Ask of each photo: if it were deleted, would the page lose a fact?

### Honesty

- NEVER present invented people, testimonials, team members or customer logos as real. NEVER use a company's logo without permission or a real relationship (see `SKILL.md`).
- When a real image will come later, fill its slot with a library photo of the subject at its final size, never visible "[Photo: …]" text or an empty tinted panel. List it in your report as a stand-in for the user's own.
- AVOID fake device, browser or editor frames around content (`tells.md`). A real screenshot may get a frame only when it needs one to be understood, and then a plain one. NEVER frame a mockup so it passes for a shipped product. Software with no screenshots: build the product's own interface in HTML, shown working, with realistic example data labelled as an example. That is content, not a mockup.
- NEVER pass off generated images as photographs of real places, products or people.

### Sourcing

- MUST use only the user's images, the project's, or photos the library prints. NEVER an image URL written from memory, and never a stock site (Unsplash, Pexels, Pixabay).
- MUST credit every library photo: one small "Photographs:" line in the footer with each printed credit.

### Art direction

- SHOULD give all photography one treatment: consistent crop ratios, color grade, light and framing. Mixed sources need grading to match, or they read as a collage.
- SHOULD crop with intent: tight crops for detail and texture, wide for place. Pick ratios from a small set and reuse them.
- SHOULD use illustration only when it has a reason (explaining something a photo can't, or a brand that owns an illustrated voice) and one consistent style, made for this product.
- AVOID mixing photography, 3D renders and flat illustration on one page.

### Icons

- SHOULD use the project's icon set if it has one (an icon package in `package.json`, an icons folder, icons imported in nearby components); never add a second. Otherwise pick one set.
- SHOULD use one icon set, one stroke weight, one size grid (for example 16/20/24px), aligned to text.
- SHOULD let icons support labels, not replace them. Icon-only buttons are for universally understood actions (close, search, menu) and MUST have an accessible name (`aria-label` or visually hidden text).
- AVOID emoji or Unicode symbols (arrows, ticks, stars) as interface icons or bullets: they render differently per platform and can't take the system's color or stroke. Allowed when emoji are part of the product's own content or voice.
- AVOID putting icons in colored tiles by default. Use an icon where it speeds recognition (navigation, file types, status), not as decoration above every heading.
- SHOULD give status icons a text equivalent; meaning is never carried by color or shape alone.

### Logos and customer marks

- SHOULD show customer or partner logos only if real and permitted. Display them at an even optical size, in one tone, unlinked unless there's a case study behind them.

## Performance

- SHOULD set `width` and `height` attributes (or `aspect-ratio`) on every image and video so the layout doesn't shift as they load.
- SHOULD serve responsive images with `srcset` and `sizes`, so phones don't download desktop files.
- SHOULD use modern formats (AVIF or WebP with a fallback via `<picture>`) for photographs; SVG for icons, logos and diagrams.
- SHOULD lazy-load images below the fold with `loading="lazy"`. Don't lazy-load the largest image in the first viewport (the LCP image); load it eagerly, and consider `fetchpriority="high"`.
- SHOULD compress: aim for under about 200KB for a full-width photo where quality allows.
- SHOULD give background video a poster image, `muted`, `playsinline`, and pause it under reduced motion (see `motion.md`).

## Alt text

- MUST give every meaningful image alt text that says what the image contributes in context, not what it literally contains ("Invoice list sorted by due date, three overdue" rather than "screenshot").
- MUST give decorative images `alt=""` so screen readers skip them.
- SHOULD keep alt to a sentence; put long explanations in a caption or nearby text. See `accessibility.md`.

## By mode

- **Persuade:** imagery is often the bold move. A page about something physical leads with a photograph, big; one strong image beats several weak ones.
- **Operate:** almost none. Icons and avatars only; empty states may use a small, consistent illustration if the system has one.
- **Read:** images serve the text: diagrams, figures, captions. Full column width or wider, never floated tiny.

## Generic defaults to catch

- **Abstract 3D shapes, isometric scenes, stock "team at laptop" photos** → see `tells.md` → decide the role, then use the real thing or nothing.
- **Fake browser or phone frames** → costume → the real screenshot, cropped to the point.
- **Icon in a rounded tile above every feature** → decoration posing as content → icons only where they aid recognition.
- **Screenshots with lorem ipsum or "John Doe"** → reads as a mockup → realistic data that fits the product.
- **Mixed image styles from different sources** → no art direction → one treatment, graded to match.

## Check

- Each image has a named role (evidence, atmosphere, explanation, identity).
- No invented people, quotes or logos; slots for images still to come look finished and are correctly sized.
- No fake device or browser chrome.
- The project's icon set if it has one, otherwise one set, one stroke weight, on a size grid; no emoji or Unicode symbol icons; icon-only buttons have accessible names.
- Every image has `width`/`height` or `aspect-ratio`; below-fold images lazy-load; the LCP image does not.
- Alt text describes purpose; decorative images have `alt=""`.
- Sources and licences are recorded.

references/interaction.md

# Interaction
